stories.title: New EU industry rules would damage UK, warns Burnham
stories.summary: The prime minister met the European Commission President during his visit to the United Nations General Assembly.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 22 September 2026

Andy Burnham has warned that planned EU rules to help European manufacturers would damage the UK, as he met European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.

The proposals aim to protect EU industry from Chinese competitors by giving companies inside the bloc priority for public contracts and subsidies.

The prime minister said he was concerned about how British industry and supply chains could be affected, and raised the subject with von der Leyen when he met her during a UN summit in New York.

Speaking on the flight to the US, Burnham also declined to rule out committing to rejoining the EU in Labour's next manifesto, saying it was an issue "for another day".

He said his immediate priority was to rebuild the relationship with the EU and reach an agreement that would boost the British economy.

The Made In Europe scheme - formally called the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA) - is yet to be finalised, but the EU's car industry has called for the UK to be included to prevent disruption to its supply chains.

Tensions over the proposed scheme have reportedly further delayed this year's planned EU-UK summit, which had already been postponed in the wake of Sir Keir Starmer's resignation as prime minister in July.

Burnham said: "We have considerable support among the member states for the position we are taking, because Europe's argument is not with us.

"We both suffer the same effects as other countries, particularly steel and the issue it raises for the steel industry in Europe and in Britain.

"We are making the argument 'we are not your enemies here… we are not the problem'. Made in Europe is dealing with a different problem.

"We are making the argument that 'let's avoid collateral damage'."

Burnham expects to find 'common ground' with Trump in first meeting Published 1 day ago

Watch: What to expect from the UN General Assembly Published 1 day ago

Ten years on, Brexit's economic impact is becoming clearer Published 14 September

Burnham told reporters his own speech to the UN General Assembly later would reflect on the decade since the Brexit vote and the "turbulence comes when outside actors seek to manipulate, to distort facts, influence the British democratic process".

"Going into the next decade, we need to be clear-eyed about that and become stronger and more on the front foot about challenging that," he said.

Asked if he would rule out making a pledge to rejoin the EU at the next general election, Burnham said: "Our focus at the moment is on a UK-EU summit which we hope will take place later this year.

"My immediate priority is to build on the good work that Keir [Starmer] did in rebuilding bridges, because those bridges were broken in the early part of this decade."

He added: "What we have got to do is now go to the next level in terms of reaching practical agreement that will further boost the British economy, and those issues are the substance of the summit alongside EU requests around youth mobility."

He said questions about rejoining the EU were for "another day".

Speaking at the Liberal Democrat conference in Brighton on Monday, the EU's new ambassador to the UK was asked whether the UK could rejoin the EU or be granted associate membership.

Jukka Salovaara said: "The doors are open but it's very much up to the UK public to identify and decide on its level of ambition when it comes to deepening cooperation with the EU."

Last September, Burnham said he would like to see the UK back in the EU in his lifetime.

Earlier this year, he said Brexit had been "damaging" but "the last thing we should do right now is re-run those arguments".

The EU has recently suggested Canada could become the bloc's first "associate member".

Asked if this could be an option for the UK, Burnham said: "The European Union made it clear that that wasn't open to us."

stories.title: Analysis: Lib Dems leave conference buoyed by Davey's message
stories.summary: Concerns over Sir Ed Davey's leadership were dampened by pledges at conference and his performance.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 22 September 2026

This was a more sombre, more serious, Sir Ed Davey.

The stunts - from falling off paddleboards to hurtling down rollercoasters – were scaled back at this year's Liberal Democrat party conference.

"This is the fight of our lives," he repeatedly told his party. The focus, much like his conference speech last year, was on Reform UK.

But the announcement he'd held back for his speech was aimed at Conservative-leaning voters: tax cuts worth billions.

And not just for lower income earners, but for those in the higher 40% rate of tax too.

Part of the announcement – raising the amount you can earn before you pay income tax altogether – was the same policy Davey's bête noire, Reform UK, announced at their conference a couple of weeks ago.

The dividing line he drew was over how it was paid for. Nigel Farage's party would reduce spending on benefits to fund the tax cut.

The Lib Dem leader said he would pay for it through the economic growth he believes could be gained by rejoining the EU's Single Market and a customs union.

Lib Dems vow to end 'computer says no' economy to boost growth Published 2 days ago

Lib Dems call for one-to-one midwife care during childbirth Published 2 days ago

Davey promises tax cuts for millions if UK rejoins EU single market Published 20 hours ago

By putting the European Union at the heart of how he would fund his tax cut, the Lib Dems couldn't be drawing a starker contrast with the Brexit-backing Reform UK and a Conservative Party also committed to cutting welfare.

But the plan is speculative. The Lib Dems insist a deal with the EU could be negotiated within a year if the party was in government after the next election.

Plenty of economic experts, including the official budget forecaster the OBR, believe the UK's economy could grow if the UK was in the Single Market.

But as recent political history teaches us, negotiating a deal with the European Union is often more difficult than party leaders hope.

And basing a tax cut on potential future economic growth is a risky business.

There is also uncertainty over whether the Lib Dems' sums add up. The independent think tank, the Institute for Fiscal Studies, said the policy as set out in the press release would cost "much more" than the £17bn the Lib Dems have budgeted for.

The party says the tax cut wouldn't come in until the fifth year after the next election. So even if the party got into power and successfully negotiated an EU deal, the tax cut could be eight years away.

But the Lib Dem MPs I spoke to afterwards were less focused on these details than the message it sent to voters.

Davey came into this conference facing criticism over his leadership from some MPs in private and others in his party in public worrying about the party's ambition and direction.

For now those concerns have been dampened. "That was the speech a lot of us have been waiting for him to give," one Davey-sceptic MP told me afterwards.

A small number are uncomfortable with the main policy from the party's conference being a tax cut that would most benefit the better off.

One told me they would rather the focus had been wooing younger voters by tackling the amount graduates repay in student loans, an old bruise for the Lib Dems.

But overall this speech, and this conference, was well received by the Lib Dem faithful.

They are a party honing their messaging before the next general election. The strategy is primarily on those 27 seats where the Lib Dems came second in 2024. Most of them are held by the Conservatives and Davey's tax cuts are aimed at appealing to those voters.

But already the attack from the Tories has been that the Lib Dems are "Labour's lapdog". That attack is in part because Davey has given his most explicit answer this week on not going into a coalition government with the Conservatives after the next general election. He's done the same for Reform UK.

But he hasn't ruled out a pact with Labour.

So that attack from the Conservatives will come again and again before the next election.

But the Lib Dems leave their Brighton conference buoyed, with sights not just on retaining their record 72 seats won at the last election, but on winning some more.

And then?

"I've got no ceiling on our ambitions," Davey said this week.

He has already served in government once, in coalition with David Cameron's Conservatives. His eyes are on another stint in office.
